I hiked 30 miles in two days with 35 pounds on my back and spent two nights in 25 to 30 degree F weather.

Ex-Post from v/hiking

It was my first winter backpacking trip. I enjoyed and learned from it. It was an awesome experience and I can't wait to get out more. Although I'm not going to lie, backpacking in warm weather is certainly preferable.

I would have liked for my base weight to have been lighter. With it being a winter trip I did need more gear than when adventuring in mild weather, and as I'm sure you all know, lighter equals more expensive in the backpacking world. Still I have some ideas, and I may detail them later when I fully unpack and reevaluate my gear. I also could have done with one less liter of water and probably about a half pound less of food.

The solitude was great. I only saw one other person the whole time.

 

Things that worked well:

  • Waterproof/Windproof Bivvy bag - I'm glad I had this to put my sleeping bag inside. I would not have been warm enough without it. My bag is rated 5 degrees F and it probably would have kept me alive at that temperature, but it was not warm enough to sleep in at 25 degrees when I tried without the bivvy. If it was windy, forget it, I would have been downright miserable without the bivvy.

  • Trekking poles - These are a must. I used for probing how deep water was, extra stability in the snow and mud, and helping ascend/descend hills it saved a lot of wear and tear on my legs.

  • Boots with gaiters - I had to cross water that was over my calf. Without these I would have been soaked. The gaiters were also great for keeping mud off my pants, which was nice since I wore all my pants in my sleeping bag.

  • Rain pants and jacket - This is the way to go, at least in the winter. A poncho would not have kept me warm and dry.

  • Neck gaiter - Extra warmth and pulled it to cover my face when needed.

  • Butt pad - I had a Z lite Sol sleeping pad with me and it's perfect sit on , keeping you warm while you eat or enjoy camp.

  • Warm food and hot coffee - I thought about going stove-less to save weight, but having a warm dinner and coffee in the morning was worth it.

  • Battery pack to recharge my phone and action camera - It was wroth the weight to be able to use these devices without having to worry about running out of battery. I listen to audio books and use my phone's camera a lot. Cell coverage was spotty, but there were times I could get internet and text/call.

 

Things that could have been better:

  • Adjustable Trekking poles - One of the poles kept sliding to different lengths. I plan on investing in a lighter weight set of fixed poles.

  • Heavy sleeping bag that wasn't warm enough - I tried the bag without the bivvy, it was too cold, even wearing all the clothing I brought (including rain pants). I need to purchase a suitable down bag.

  • Cotton hoodie mid layer - This wasn't awful, I kept it dry so it kept me warm, but I want something lighter, not really sure what.

  • Sleeping pads - I brought the Neoair Xlite and Z-Lite Sol. I like the Sol because it is a seat too, but it is bulky and not warm enough by itself. In fact the two put together were barely warm enough. I had to keep the Sol in my pack otherwise it interfered with my rain cover, and that takes up a ton of space. I need to look at other options.

Very cool and thanks for the update. I have two questions:

  1. Footwear. 15ish miles a day isn't a short trek. Tips? Advice? Brands or gotchas?

  2. Pack straps. My shoulders do what's called "nontraumatic dislocation." Basically, the only thing keeping my shoulders together is muscle strength (requires surgery and therapy to fix). Having just lugged a decent amount of weight for that distance, what advice, things to look for, gotchas and thoughts do you have?

Taking care of your feet is paramount for sure.

I used Vasque's Snowburban II UltraDry Boot, paired with Carhartt baselayer socks (Olefin/Nylon), and People's socks (Wool /Nylon).

The boots are awesome. No break in needed for me. I hiked in them prior to my trip and they never bothered my feet from the start. They are warm and did not leak when crossing brooks and streams (gaiters helped for sure).

I also carry a Trail Toes anti friction cream and leukotape. I apply Trail Toes to the toes at the start of each day. The leukotape can go directly onto toes if you do start getting preblister friction. At the start of the second day my small toes were a bit red and tender so I used the tape.

If you ever start getting discomfort STOP and examine your feet. I cannot stress this enough. Even if it is slight, it is worth the inconvenience to take off your boots and socks. Hiking with a blister is the worst.

I carry the Swiss Army Classic SD knife. It has scissors and a nail file in case I need to trim a toe nail that digging into my skin.

The hip belt on your pack is key to taking load off your shoulders. You can transfer more weight to your hips by keeping the shoulder straps a bit loose. I tend to tighten and loosen straps to shift weight from shoulders to hips and back, giving one a break while the other carries more of the load. I don't know if this is best practice or not, but that's what seems to work for me.

Other than that just keeping your body in shape. I'm not a body builder by any stretch, but I do some work outs to keep my traps and other shoulder muscles in shape.
